prompt:
A team is considering a weekly meeting, but its members already feel overloaded. Explain how to decide whether a meeting is the right tool. A response of around 120 words is enough.

Write the requested response as one self-contained paragraph of plain text. Do not use a title, headings, bullet points, numbered lists, Markdown formatting, code fences, or line breaks. Include only the requested content, without any introductory or closing commentary from the assistant. Keep the approximate word target given in the task. If the task calls for an email, dialogue, steps, or calculations, express that content within the same paragraph.
base_prompt: A team is considering a weekly meeting, but its members already feel overloaded. Explain how to decide whether a meeting is the right tool. A response of around 120 words is enough.
text: Before scheduling a weekly meeting, clarify the problem it is meant to solve. Ask whether the team needs shared decisions, rapid coordination, problem-solving, or relationship-building that cannot be handled effectively through written updates or an occasional meeting. Define the specific outcomes participants should achieve and identify who genuinely needs to attend. Estimate the meeting’s total cost, including preparation and lost focus time, then compare it with the expected benefits. Consider lighter alternatives first, such as an asynchronous status update, shared dashboard, decision log, or shorter meeting triggered only when issues arise. If a meeting seems justified, run a time-limited trial with a clear agenda, required preparation, strict duration, and an explicit cancellation rule. Review afterward whether it produced valuable outcomes and adjust or stop it if not.
